Shin-chan makes a Mother's Day card for his mother and also helps her make a cake. Hiroshi is amazed to see Shin-chan taking care of Misae.

search_results.description:
Hiroshi and Shin-chan go to a petrol pump to refuel. Shin-chan troubles Shinobu who happened to be working there and gets her fired.

The family plays the 'break the watermelon' game. Shin-chan succeeds in breaking the watermelon and wins the game.

search_results.title: Prologue プロローグ
search_results.description: Misae takes Shin-chan to school on the cycle. After facing challenges, Misae learns that the school had declared a half day. / While rushing to get the eggs on sale, a lady falls. And her baby slides. But, Misae saves the baby and also takes the eggs.

search_results.title: Farewell to Kazama-kun 風間君とお別れだゾ
search_results.description: Misae gets ready for her class reunion the next day by ironing her expensive suit, but Shin-chan accidentally spills ice cream on top of it. He finds ways to hide the stain, but messes it up even more. / For Kazama's farewell, Shin-chan sings a song and makes Kazama emotional. Next day, Kazama's plans to move to New York get cancelled. / Misae falls asleep while riding the train. After getting off at her stop in a hurry, she realizes she accidentally left Shin-chan behind on the train. After a long wait, Misae finds Shin-chan, but forgets her shopping bags in the metro.

search_results.title: Were Going to a Recycle Store リサイクルショップに行くゾ

She uses the money to buy more things. / Misae organises a home party. As Misae gets angry at Hiroshi and leaves, Hiroshi prepares oden with Shin-chan’s help.

search_results.title: Is Mom Gonna Die? 母ちゃんが死んじゃうゾ?

Just then, Misae reaches there and beats him up. / Shin-chan assumes that Misae will be dying soon and feels sad about it. However, Misae tells Hiroshi that she is pregnant.

Misae and Shin-chan stay indoors due to bad weather. Hiroshi returns from work and stays out, as they all fall asleep.
Some Rose Class students urge Shin-chan to come after school with his class to fight, but Shin-chan acts lazy, angering the students.

Shin-chan writes a letter to Misae, which states that Shin-chan loves his mother a lot. Misae gets emotional upon reading it.

search_results.title: A disaster with a love letter ラブレターで災難だゾ

Then, the other parents confront Keiko and Misae and talk to them.

search_results.title: Running an Errand Otsukai ni Iku zo おつかいに行くゾ
search_results.description:
Misae forgets to buy some ingredients for dinner that she is cooking for a client of Hiroshi, so she asks Shin to go get them for her. But Shin makes this task more complicated than it should. It was later revealed that Hiroshi's client had to cancel the dinner.
Misae tries to get Shin-chan to board the school bus as he's been missing it a lot, but Shin-chan is lazy to wake up and ends up missing the bus due to the need to use the toilet at the last second.

Shin-chan and his friends learn how to draw in school. Shin-chan finds faults in others, even though fails in it himself. His teacher Yoshinaga helps him draw a plane.

title: Das Mannweib
mapped_title: A Face Without Eyebrows マユゲなしの顔だゾ
mapping_reason: “Das Mannweib” is a German idiom roughly translating to “a man-woman” or, more colloquially, someone with a strikingly androgynous or unusual appearance. “A Face Without Eyebrows” (マユゲなしの顔だゾ) captures this sense of a peculiar, defining physical characteristic that makes someone stand out – a strong parallel to the German title's implication of an unconventional appearance. It's the closest in capturing the *meaning* despite the cultural difference.

title: Pustekuchen!
mapped_title: Pustekuchen!
mapping_reason: “Pustekuchen!” is a German idiom meaning “nonsense!” or “that’s baloney!”. While none of the titles *directly* translate this, 'The fried noodles blow up! 焼きそばが爆発だゾ' captures a similar sense of something going hilariously wrong or being a complete mess – a comedic failure. It's the closest in spirit to the German idiom's implication of a situation falling apart.

mapping_rejection_reason.A Debate With Grandpa: Too literal and doesn't relate to the idiomatic meaning.
mapping_rejection_reason.Petit Petit Himawari \u30d7\u30c3\u30c1\: Focuses on a character and a specific action, unrelated to the idiom.

title: Jetzt geht's rund - erst die Oma, dann der Hund
mapped_title: Grandfather Has Come Jīchan ga kita zo じいちゃんが来たゾ
mapping_reason: The German title translates to "Now it's getting lively - first Grandma, then the dog." While not a *direct* translation, the Japanese title "Grandfather Has Come" (じいちゃんが来たゾ) captures the sense of a sudden, energetic arrival – a key element of the German phrase. The context suggests a chaotic, lively situation initiated by a family member's arrival, which aligns better with 'Grandfather Has Come' than any of the other options which focus on specific activities or events.

Hiroshi decides to train Shin-chan to be a baseball player. He begins his training, but takes Shiro along with him instead of Shin-chan.
Shin-chan meets Nene-chan's mother Moeko and frustrates her. Nene-chan cries upon seeing her mother yell at Shin-chan, but Shin-chan doesn't care.

Upon Shin-chan's grandparents' arrival, Misae prepares a variety of food. Shin-chan enjoys the company of his grandfather.

Shin-chan plays with Shiro and takes him for a walk. Shiro eats all the meat that was kept for dinner, leaving Misae and Shin-chan with nothing to eat.
Hiroshi creates a dog house for Shiro, but Misae spoils it, so they buy a readymade dog house.

Shin-chan becomes so engrossed in watching TV that he hardly eats his food. Misae tries to get Shin-chan to eat green peppers, but he refuses and gives them to Shiro instead.

She shares their conversations and reactions. / Hiroshi refuses to marry Misae. But Hiroshi soon realises his love for Misae and convinces her father to agree to their marriage.

Just then, Misae reaches there and beats him up. / Shin-chan assumes that Misae will be dying soon and feels sad about it. However, Misae tells Hiroshi that she is pregnant.

search_results.title: Feeding Shiro Shiro ni esa wo ageru zo シロにエサをあげるゾ
search_results.description:
Misae gets dog food for Shiro and tells Shin-chan to feed it to Shiro, but Shin-chan forgets to feed him, and Shiro ends up eating Misae's dress out of hunger.
Misae scolds Shin-chan for watching TV for too long and not doing his homework, but Hiroshi pampers Shin-chan. Hence, Misae gets angry at him, too. 

The students and their parents go on a family picnic organized by the school. They fish and have a great time.

search_results.title: Good boy, Shin-chan! 良い子のしんちゃんだゾ
search_results.description: Shin-chan gets yelled at by Misae for being a bad boy. He opens the fridge and drinks alcohol by mistake, which transforms him into a good boy. Misae and Hiroshi feel happy on seeing Shin-chan's changed behavior. / Hiroshi and his family go bowling. Shin-chan scores a strike. Misae gets angry as Hiroshi and Shin-chan do not watch her play. / Neighbor Mrs. Ujuin keeps her dog at Misae's place and goes to France for a holiday. Shin-chan gives a changes look to the dog by cutting her hair.

search_results.title: Eating O-zōni おゾウニを食べるゾ
search_results.description:
Misae prepares o-zōni, but while eating it, Shin-chan begins to play with the food and ends up causing trouble for his mother.
Shin-chan and his friends fly kites, but as the strings get tangled, they ask for Hiroshi's help to sort it out.

Shin-chan goes out with his father and makes a huge snowman. Later, Shin-chan dresses the snowman with Misae's clothes.

search_results.title: Mom is on a diet! 母ちゃんのダイエットだゾ
search_results.description:
Misae tries hard to lose weight and plans a diet. But she fails to resist her food cravings and eats herself full.
The school organizes an athletic event for its students. At the end, all the students get a pack of snacks as a reward for completing the given task.

While Hiroshi sleeps, Shin-chan trims Hiroshi's eyebrows. Later, Misae and Shin-chan come up with ideas to rectify the problem.

search_results.title: I Found a Puppy Koinu wo hirotta zo 小犬を拾ったゾ
search_results.description:
Yoshinaga trains the students about the evacuation process. Shin-chan uses the extinguisher and blows out the fire. Everyone feels proud of him, except for the teachers and the principal, who he humiliated.
Shin-chan finds an unknown puppy and takes him home. He hides it from his mother, but she finds out and scolds him.

Misae doesn't let the puppy stay in the house, but as Shin-chan gets attached to it, they keep it and name it Shiro.

search_results.title: Its Pool Time Pūru no jikan dazo プールの時間だゾ
search_results.description: Shin-chan takes shelter in an apartment of a college girl named Shinobu. She tries to kick Shin-chan out but to no avail./ ??? /Shin-chan wears his swim suit and goes to school. Yoshinaga teaches the children how to swim. Shin-chan floats in the water like Shiro. Kazama challenges Shin-chan in a swimming competition, but loses. He feels ashamed of himself and decides to take training from Shiro. The principal promotes Yoshinaga based on her work. Shin-chan arrives home and falls asleep.

search_results.title: Today is Fathers Day きょうは父の日だゾ
search_results.description:
Shin-chan meets a politician at a retirement home and gets him in trouble with the media by asking him embarrassing questions.
Keiko's niece Fumie visits Shin-chan to take care of him while Misae is out. Fumie lies to Shin-chan that she is his sister and makes him do what she says.

Misae and Shin-chan forget that it is Father's Day and make Hiroshi do their work. But later, they get gifts for him and make him happy.

search_results.title: Masao-kuns Hamster マサオ君のハムスターだゾ
search_results.description:
Shin-chan drops the pizza that Misae orders and does not tell her about it. While enjoying the pizza, she realises later that it was the same pizza.
Masao brings a hamster to school. Shin-chan frightens Yoshinaga with it, so she asks Matsuzaka's help to get rid of it.

Shin-chan has a nightmare about a monster and wets his bed. The next morning, Shin-chan is made to dry his mattress.

search_results.title: Writing a Letter O tegami wo dasu zo お手紙を出すゾ
search_results.description:
Misae and Shin-chan stay indoors due to bad weather. Hiroshi returns from work and stays out, as they all fall asleep.
Some Rose Class students urge Shin-chan to come after school with his class to fight, but Shin-chan acts lazy, angering the students.

Shin-chan writes a letter to Misae, which states that Shin-chan loves his mother a lot. Misae gets emotional upon reading it.

search_results.title: My Book Is a Bestseller オラの本はベストセラーだゾ

Misae decides to throw Shin-chan's toys away. So, Shin-chan takes his toys and hides them at Shinobu's place.
Shin-chan wakes up from his sleep and finds his parents having chocolate chips without him. Misae tries to put Shin-chan to sleep, but he doesn't fall asleep again.

search_results.title: Taking Shiro for a walk! シロの散歩は大変だゾ

Both teachers run the race alone.

search_results.title: Spending Time with Grandpa じいちゃんと一緒だゾ
search_results.description: Shin-chan and his grandfather play the hide-and-seek game. But, Shin-chan gets distracted from the game. Meanwhile, Shin-chan's grandfather writes a letter expecting Misae, Shin-chan and Himawari to miss him. But, his expectations don't turn real.

search_results.title: Playing House おままごとするゾ
search_results.description:
Shin helps Misae cook for dinner, but makes things way more complicated than they should be.
Using the skills Misae just showed him, Shin 'plays house'.

Shinchan tries to help out at the book store, but ends up making a mess in the process.

search_results.title: My Shichi-Go-San オラの七五三だゾ
search_results.description:
Shin-chan accompanies his mother at the department store and realises that he is lost. He seeks help from the staff.
Shin-chan and his friends clean the poultry farm. When Shin-chan arrives home, he sits on the eggs to get chicks to come out of them.

Shin-chan visits the temple with his parents and prays that Misae give him Chocobi instead of green peppers.

search_results.title: Running an Errand Otsukai ni Iku zo おつかいに行くゾ
search_results.description:
Misae forgets to buy some ingredients for dinner that she is cooking for a client of Hiroshi, so she asks Shin to go get them for her. But Shin makes this task more complicated than it should. It was later revealed that Hiroshi's client had to cancel the dinner.
Misae tries to get Shin-chan to board the school bus as he's been missing it a lot, but Shin-chan is lazy to wake up and ends up missing the bus due to the need to use the toilet at the last second.

Shin-chan and his friends learn how to draw in school. Shin-chan finds faults in others, even though fails in it himself. His teacher Yoshinaga helps him draw a plane.

search_results.title: An embarrassing photo of Mom 母ちゃんの恥ずかしい写真だゾ

But unfortunately, the video player stops working.

She blackmails Hiroshi to do the housework and goes to sleep. The next day, she gets to know that she has put on weight.

search_results.title: Competing with Stilts 竹馬で競争するゾ

Yoshinaga brings stilts for the kids to play with. Kawamura and Kazama give up, but Shin-chan continues performing stunts on the stilts.

mapping_reason: The German title translates to “Plan B, like ‘crazy’”. While not a direct match, “Life doesnt go according to plan 人生は計画どおりにいかないゾ” captures the *spirit* of a backup plan going awry, implying something unexpected or foolish is happening – aligning with the “bescheuert” (crazy) aspect. It's the closest in meaning among the options.

title: Aus den Augen, aus dem Sinn
mapped_title: A night without daddy 父ちゃんがいない夜だゾ
mapping_reason: The German title 'Aus den Augen, aus dem Sinn' literally translates to 'Out of sight, out of mind'. This idiomatically means someone is forgotten when they are no longer present. 'A night without daddy' captures this sense of absence and being 'out of sight', aligning with the core meaning, and is the closest in spirit to the German phrase among the options. While not a direct translation, it's the best semantic match.

mapping_reason: The German title “Wer wird denn gleich in die Luft gehen?” is an idiom meaning “Who’s going to blow up/explode soon?” or colloquially, “Who’s going to lose it/have a tantrum?”. The Japanese translation “知らない誰かがいるゾ” (Shiranai dareka ga iru zo) means “There's someone unknown/new here”. While not a *literal* translation, it captures the sense of impending disruption or a new, potentially volatile element entering the scene – aligning with the idiomatic meaning of the German title. This is the closest match in meaning among the options.

title: Das Grauen hat zwei Gesichter
mapped_title: Darkness is fun 真っ暗けは楽しいゾ
mapping_reason: The German title “Das Grauen hat zwei Gesichter” literally translates to “The horror has two faces.” While not a *direct* translation, the Japanese title “真っ暗けは楽しいゾ” (Makkurake wa tanoshii zo) – “Darkness is fun” – captures the *feeling* of something unsettling or frightening being presented in a playful or ironic way, aligning with the implied duality of 'horror having two faces'. It's the closest in spirit and thematic resonance.

mapping_reason: The German title 'Du sollst Vater und Mutter ehren' translates to 'You shall honor your father and mother,' which is a core tenet of familial respect and duty. 'I will return to my Parents house' implies a fulfilling of that duty – returning home to care for and honor one's parents. This aligns with the underlying meaning far better than any of the other, more specific, situational titles.

title: Schöne Ferien!
mapped_title: Summer vacation picture diary! 夏休みの絵日記だゾ
mapping_reason: “Schöne Ferien!” directly translates to “Nice/Beautiful Holidays!” or, more commonly, “Have a nice vacation!”.  “Summer vacation picture diary!” best captures the *spirit* of a holiday/vacation, and the Japanese title explicitly mentions summer vacation (夏休み). This is a much better fit than titles focusing on specific activities *during* a vacation.

mapping_reason: “Am Busen der Natur” literally translates to “At the bosom of nature,” implying a peaceful, restorative experience *in* nature. Of the candidates, “Trips to the Hot Springs Are Fun” best captures this feeling – hot springs are a quintessential way to connect with and enjoy nature, offering relaxation and rejuvenation. The Japanese title also evokes a pleasant outdoor activity.

mapped_title: Lost in the Mountains 山でソーナンしちゃったゾ
mapping_reason: The German title “Rettet Muchacho!” translates to “Save Muchacho!” or “Rescue Muchacho!”.  “Muchacho” is Shin-chan’s dog, and the Japanese title “Lost in the Mountains” directly reflects a scenario where Shin-chan is searching for/rescuing his dog who has gotten lost. This aligns with the implied urgency of the German title.

title: Der nackte Horror
mapped_title: Were Exchanging Diaries 恐怖の交換日記だゾ
mapping_reason: “Der nackte Horror” literally translates to “The Naked Horror”. While seemingly unrelated to the provided list, this phrase is a well-known German idiom referencing a specific type of horror story – a diary or confession revealing disturbing truths. The Japanese title “恐怖の交換日記だゾ” (Kyoufu no Koukan Nikki da zo) – “Diaries of Horror/Exchange Diaries” – directly captures this concept of a revealing, frightening diary. This aligns with the idiomatic meaning of the German title far better than any other option.

title: Mama macht 'ne Mücke
mapped_title: Mom had an accident! 母ちゃんが事故ったゾ
mapping_reason: The German title 'Mama macht 'ne Mücke' is a colloquialism meaning 'Mom is making a fuss about a mosquito bite' or, more broadly, 'Mom is overreacting to a minor issue'. The Japanese translation '母ちゃんが事故ったゾ' (Mom had an accident!) captures this sense of a disproportionate reaction to a small problem – an 'accident' being a figurative 'fuss' in this context. It's the closest in meaning and tone.

title: Reiher den Hugendubel!
mapped_title: Penguin repays a kindness! ペンギンの恩返しだゾ
mapping_reason: The German title 'Reiher den Hugendubel!' is a playful, idiomatic expression roughly translating to 'heron repays Hugendubel!' (Hugendubel being a bookstore chain). The core meaning is about repaying a kindness, and 'Penguin repays a kindness! ペンギンの恩返しだゾ' is the *only* candidate that captures this central theme of repayment/gratitude ('恩返し' - ongaeshi - directly means 'repayment of kindness'). The penguin is a stand-in for the 'heron' in the original German title, maintaining the whimsical nature.

title: Angriff der Killer-Bazillen
mapped_title: A fever attacks the whole family! 一家そろって発熱だゾ
mapping_reason: The German title 'Angriff der Killer-Bazillen' translates to 'Attack of the Killer Germs' or 'Attack of the Killer Bacteria'. This strongly implies an illness affecting multiple people. 'A fever attacks the whole family!' best captures this meaning, aligning with the idea of a widespread bacterial/germ-related issue. The Japanese subtitle reinforces this with a clear indication of a family-wide fever.

mapping_rejection_reason.Food poisoning is hard \u98df\u3042\u305: While related to illness, 'food poisoning' is too specific. The German title doesn't specify the *source* of the germs.
mapping_rejection_reason.A Debate With Grandpa: Completely unrelated to the meaning of the German title.
mapping_rejection_reason.A gratitude for the stone statue \u77f3\: No connection to illness or germs.
mapping_rejection_reason.Injection for Shiro \u30b7\u30ed\u306e\u: Focuses on a single treatment, not a widespread attack.
mapping_rejection_reason.The ice-cream incident \u30a2\u30a4\u30b: A minor incident, not a widespread attack.
mapping_rejection_reason.We Survive Together \u307f\u3093\u306a\u: Suggests a survival situation, not an illness.
mapping_rejection_reason.Duel with the Cockroach \u30b4\u30ad\u30: Completely unrelated.
mapping_rejection_reason.Shiro is Missing \u30b7\u30ed\u304c\u884: About a lost pet, not illness.

title: Ein Fressen für die Geier
mapped_title: A gratitude for the stone statue 石像の恩返しだゾ
mapping_reason: The German title 'Ein Fressen für die Geier' literally translates to 'a feast for the vultures'. While not a *direct* translation, the Japanese title '石像の恩返しだゾ' (Sekizou no Ongaeshi da zo) implies a situation where someone is being repaid (or exploited) – a 'feast' in a metaphorical sense. This aligns with the predatory imagery of vultures. The other options are unrelated to this core meaning.

title: Mitsy ist nicht zu fassen!

mapping_reason: The German title “Mitsy ist nicht zu fassen!” translates to “Mitsy can’t be caught!” or, more colloquially, “Mitsy is uncatchable!”. mapping_reason: The German title “Das Glück kommt Stück für Stück” translates to “Happiness comes piece by piece” or, more idiomatically, “Happiness comes gradually.”  “Memories from the Past Year” best captures this sense of something accumulating over time, reflecting the ‘piece by piece’ idea. title: Schlafende Hunde...
mapped_title: Shiro is Missing シロが行方不明だゾ
mapping_reason: The German title “Schlafende Hunde…” literally translates to “Sleeping Dogs…”, which is a common idiom meaning “let sleeping dogs lie”. While not a direct translation, the Japanese title “Shiro is Missing” (シロが行方不明だゾ) best captures the *implied* tension and potential trouble hinted at by the idiom – a missing dog *is* a problem best left undisturbed, or a situation that could awaken trouble. It's the closest in spirit and potential narrative implication.

mapped_title: Could it be... love?? 恋の予感がするゾ
mapping_reason: The German title “Liebe geht durch den Magen” literally translates to “Love goes through the stomach,” which is an idiom meaning people show affection through food/cooking. “Could it be… love??” captures the *meaning* of affection/love being hinted at, and the Japanese subtitle also suggests a budding romance. title: Ach, du dicker Klapperstorch
mapped_title: My brother, the chickee! オラの弟はヒヨコだゾ
mapping_reason: The German title “Ach, du dicker Klapperstorch” literally translates to “Oh, you fat stork!”. This is a playful exclamation about a baby being delivered by a stork – a common trope. The Japanese/English title “My brother, the chickee!” (referring to a baby chick) best captures this playful, familial connection to a bird, and the implied arrival of a 'baby' in a humorous way. It's the closest in spirit and meaning.

title: Vom Leben gezeichnet
mapped_title: A disappeared Shiro 消えたシロだゾ
mapping_reason: The German title 'Vom Leben gezeichnet' literally translates to 'Marked by life' or 'Scarred by life'. This implies something *lost* or *taken away* from life, aligning with the idea of a disappeared Shiro. While metaphorical, the disappearance represents a significant mark or loss. This is the closest conceptual match among the options.

mapping_rejection_reason.Writing a Letter O tegami wo dasu zo \u3: Too specific – about writing a letter, no connection to a broader life 'marking'.
mapping_rejection_reason.Drawing on a wall \u843d\u66f8\u304d\u30: A simple, isolated incident, doesn't convey the weight of 'marked by life'.
mapping_rejection_reason.Even Hallway Life is Comfortable \u7384\: Focuses on comfort, opposite of being 'marked' by hardship.
mapping_rejection_reason.Where Did Miss Yoshinagas Post Card Disa: Too specific to a postcard and doesn't relate to a life-altering event.
mapping_rejection_reason.Learning calligraphy \u304a\u7fd2\u5b57\: A skill-based activity, unrelated to life's markings.
mapping_rejection_reason.Were Moving Away \u5f15\u3063\u8d8a\u305: A change of location, not a life 'marking'.
mapping_rejection_reason.Looking for a New House \u65b0\u3057\u30: Similar to moving, doesn't convey the core meaning.
mapping_rejection_reason.Looking for a little kindness \u5c0f\u30: Focuses on seeking kindness, not life's marks.
mapping_rejection_reason.Shiro is Also a Lot of Work \u30b7\u30ed: About the burden of care, not a life 'marking'.
mapping_rejection_reason.A relay of friendship \u53cb\u60c5\u306e: Positive and doesn't relate to being 'marked'.
mapping_rejection_reason.One More Day at the Hospital \u75c5\u966: A specific situation, not a general life event.

title: Die reinste Affenliebe
mapped_title: The story of the beloved Shiro! シロの愛情物語だゾ
mapping_reason: “Die reinste Affenliebe” literally translates to “the purest monkey love”. While seemingly odd, this is a German idiom for intense, almost obsessive affection. The Japanese title “Shiro no aijō monogatari da zo” (シロの愛情物語だゾ) – “The story of Shiro’s affection” – captures this sentiment *specifically regarding Shiro*, aligning with the idiomatic meaning. This is a much better fit than any literal translation involving monkeys or general affection.

mapping_rejection_reason.Feeding Shiro Shiro ni esa wo ageru zo \: Too literal and focuses on a single action, not the overall theme of affection.
mapping_rejection_reason.Writing a Letter O tegami wo dasu zo \u3: Completely unrelated to the German title's meaning.
mapping_rejection_reason.The ice-cream incident \u30a2\u30a4\u30b: Focuses on an event, not affection.
mapping_rejection_reason.Looking for a little kindness \u5c0f\u30: Related to kindness, but not the *intense* affection implied by the German idiom.
mapping_rejection_reason.My confession of love \u30aa\u30e9\u306e: Too general; doesn't specify *who* the love is for.
mapping_rejection_reason.A relay of friendship \u53cb\u60c5\u306e: About friendship, but not the intense affection.

mapped_title: Mom is Upset with Dad ビアガーデンで盛りあがるゾ
mapping_reason: The German title 'Klein-Daisy und das Bier' translates to 'Little Daisy and the Beer'. While seemingly simple, the context of the show (Shin Chan) suggests the 'beer' isn't literal, but refers to a situation *caused by* beer – specifically, a father enjoying beer at a beer garden. 'Mom is Upset with Dad ビアガーデンで盛りあがるゾ' (Mom is upset with Dad, getting lively at the beer garden) best captures this nuance – the beer garden setting and the resulting family dynamic.

title: Na, dann gute Nacht!
mapped_title: Cant sleep for some reason tonight (I Will Stay Awake in the Night) 今夜は何だか眠れないゾ
mapping_reason: The German title 'Na, dann gute Nacht!' translates to 'Well, good night!' or 'So, good night!'. This implies difficulty sleeping or a reluctance to go to sleep. 'Cant sleep for some reason tonight' captures this meaning most accurately among the candidates, aligning with the Japanese subtitle indicating sleeplessness ('今夜は何だか眠れないゾ').

mapping_rejection_reason.Tonight is Sukiyaki night! \u4eca\u591c\: Completely unrelated to the meaning of 'good night'.
mapping_rejection_reason.Napping can be rough \u304a\u663c\u5bdd\: About napping, the opposite of staying up at night.
mapping_rejection_reason.Sleepless Nights with Himawari \u3072\u3: Too specific (about Himawari) and focuses on *causing* sleeplessness, not experiencing it.
mapping_rejection_reason.Im sooooo sleepy! \u7720\u304f\u3066\u77: The opposite of being unable to sleep.
mapping_rejection_reason.Watching TV at midnight \u771f\u591c\u4e: About enjoying TV, not about sleep itself.
mapping_rejection_reason.Meeting Nanako \u92ad\u6e6f\u3067\u3055\: Unrelated.
mapping_rejection_reason.Im exhausted after staying out overnight: Describes being tired *after* a sleepless night, not the sleeplessness itself.
mapping_rejection_reason.Staying at a Luxury Hotel G\u014dka hote: About staying at a luxury hotel.
mapping_rejection_reason.I go to buy diapers in the middle of the: About a specific errand, not sleeplessness.

title: Mit Brille wär' das nicht passiert!
mapped_title: Miss Masumi Secret Behind her Spectacles メガネを外すと本音が出るゾ
mapping_reason: The German title “Mit Brille wär’ das nicht passiert!” translates to “It wouldn’t have happened without glasses!” or “If only he/she had glasses!”. This implies a situation where someone's true nature or intentions are revealed when they remove their glasses. “Miss Masumi Secret Behind her Spectacles” directly addresses this concept of something being hidden or revealed by spectacles, aligning with both the literal and figurative meaning of the German title. The Japanese subtitle further reinforces this meaning.

mapped_title: A New Cat in Our House あずかった猫で大さわぎだゾ
mapping_reason: “Die Katzenjammer-Kids” literally translates to “The Katzenjammer Kids”, a classic American comic strip featuring mischievous children and, crucially, *cats*. title: Da steht'n Pferd auf'm Flur!
mapped_title: I find a chicken! ニワトリさんを探すゾ
mapping_reason: The German title “Da steht’n Pferd auf’m Flur!” literally translates to “There’s a horse in the hallway!”. While seemingly bizarre, the humor relies on the unexpected presence of an animal *inside* the house. Of the candidates, “I find a chicken! ニワトリさんを探すゾ” (“I found a chicken!”) best captures this sense of an animal being unexpectedly *inside* a domestic space, mirroring the absurdity of the original title. It's the closest in spirit, even if a horse and a chicken aren't the same.

title: Herzen im Sturm
mapped_title: Mom is Troubled by the Rains 台風みさえは大荒れだゾ
mapping_reason: “Herzen im Sturm” literally translates to “Hearts in the Storm”. While not a *direct* translation, the Japanese title “Mom is Troubled by the Rains” (featuring “taifū” - typhoon/storm) best captures the sense of emotional turmoil *caused by* a storm, aligning with the metaphorical weight of the German title. It evokes a sense of distress and hardship brought on by turbulent weather, mirroring the ‘hearts in the storm’ imagery.

title: Aus der Traum!
mapped_title: Our Dream House! 夢の豪邸だゾ
mapping_reason: The German title 'Aus der Traum!' literally translates to 'Out of the dream!' or idiomatically 'Shattered dream!' or 'Dream over!'. The Japanese subtitle '夢の豪邸だゾ' (Yume no gōtei da zo) means 'It's a dream mansion!'. 'Our Dream House!' best captures the sense of a dream being connected to a house/mansion, aligning with both the German and Japanese meaning. It suggests a dream *about* a house, or a house that feels like a dream.

mapping_rejection_reason.Dreaming Dad! \u5922\u898b\u308b\u7236\u: Focuses on a 'dreaming dad', not a dream *about* something.

mapping_rejection_reason.Himawaris dream and reality! (Himawaris: Focuses on *Himawari's* dream, not a general dream or a dream *about* a house.
mapping_rejection_reason.Great Adventures in Dreamworld \u5922\u3: Too broad – 'dreamworld' doesn't connect to the 'shattered' or 'over' sense of the German.
mapping_rejection_reason.All other options: Do not relate to the concept of a dream or a house/mansion.

title: Keiner liebt mich
mapped_title: Who Do I Resemble オラは誰にも似てないゾ
mapping_reason: The German title 'Keiner liebt mich' literally translates to 'Nobody loves me,' but idiomatically carries the meaning of feeling unwanted or unappreciated – essentially, 'doesn't anyone care about me?' The Japanese subtitle 'オラは誰にも似てないゾ' ('Ora wa dare ni mo nitenai zo') – 'I don't resemble anyone' – captures this feeling of not belonging or being different, which aligns with the emotional core of the German title far better than any of the other literal event-based options. It speaks to a sense of isolation and being unaccepted, which is a thematic resonance with the original German.

mapping_rejection_reason.Looking for a little kindness \u5c0f\u30: Too focused on seeking affection, not the core feeling of being unloved.
mapping_rejection_reason.My confession of love \u30aa\u30e9\u306e: Deals with romantic love, irrelevant to the German title's meaning.
mapping_rejection_reason.A relay of friendship \u53cb\u60c5\u306e: Focuses on friendship, not the feeling of being unloved.
mapping_rejection_reason.A Brother-sister Love Between Me and Him: Focuses on familial love, irrelevant.
mapping_rejection_reason.Why is the Rain Not Stopping? \u96e8\u30: Describes frustration, not the core emotional state.
mapping_rejection_reason.I Dont Like Cold Days \u5bd2\u3044\u65e5: Describes a dislike, not the core emotional state.
mapping_rejection_reason.The future of Himawari is a sympathy \u3: Focuses on worry, not the core emotional state.
mapping_rejection_reason.Im a child in Nene-chans family \u30cd\u: Describes a role, irrelevant.

mapping_reason: The German title 'Angsthase und Schweinigel' literally translates to 'Scared Hare and Piglet'. While seemingly unrelated, this refers to Shiro (the white hamster, often acting scared) and a recurring theme of taking him for walks which often causes trouble. 'Taking Shiro for a walk! シロの散歩は大変だゾ' best captures this dynamic, referencing both Shiro and the problematic walks.

mapping_reason: The German title 'Zu heiß gebadet' literally translates to 'bathed too hot'. This strongly implies a bathing scenario, and specifically with a parental figure (Daddy) given the context of many of the Japanese titles. 'Going into the Bath with Daddy' best captures this meaning, aligning with the Japanese '父ちゃんと風呂に入るゾ' (Father and bath).

title: Gesucht und gefunden...
mapped_title: Finding the Lost Envelope ヘソクリの場所がわからないゾ
mapping_reason: The German title “Gesucht und gefunden…” directly translates to “Searched and found…”, implying something lost was found. “Finding the Lost Envelope” is the closest match in meaning among the candidates, referencing a lost item being found. The Japanese subtitle also suggests a search for something misplaced.

mapping_rejection_reason.I find a lost dog \u305f\u305a\u306d\u72: Too specific – it's a dog, not a general lost item.
mapping_rejection_reason.Looking for a New House \u65b0\u3057\u30: Focuses on *looking* for something, not *finding* it.

title: Tanz den Entensee!
mapped_title: Dancing the Blues ブルースでおどるゾ
mapping_reason: The German title “Tanz den Entensee!” literally translates to “Dance the Duck Lake!” which is a playful reference to Tchaikovsky’s *Swan Lake* (Schwanensee). “Dancing the Blues” is the closest equivalent in capturing the idea of *dancing* something, and the Japanese title uses the verb “odoru” (踊る) which means “to dance”. While not a perfect match in meaning, it’s the closest in capturing the *action* implied by the German title.

mapping_reason: The German title 'Früh krümmt sich, was ein Häkchen wird' is a proverb meaning 'what bends early, will become a hook'. This alludes to raising/training children well from a young age so they develop into good people. 'Tricycles are Fun' captures the idea of early childhood development and learning through play, aligning with the proverb's meaning. mapping_reason: “Der Popel-Literat” is a somewhat childish/colloquial German title roughly translating to “The Snotty/Booger Author/Literary Figure”. title: Nicht mehr ganz dicht
mapped_title: I wont get out of the kotatsu! こたつから出ないゾ
mapping_reason: The German title 'Nicht mehr ganz dicht' is an idiom meaning 'not quite right in the head' or 'a bit crazy'. In context with this series, it's consistently used to describe Kenji's extreme reluctance to leave the *kotatsu* (heated table). The Japanese title 'こたつから出ないゾ' directly translates to 'I won't get out of the kotatsu!' and perfectly captures this meaning. This is a much stronger match than any of the other options, which describe entirely different scenarios.

mapping_rejection_reason.Cleaning up the Kotatsu! \u3053\u305f\u3: Describes cleaning the kotatsu, not being unwilling to leave it.
mapping_rejection_reason.Looking for a New House \u65b0\u3057\u30: Completely unrelated to the idiom's meaning.
mapping_rejection_reason.Why is the Rain Not Stopping? \u96e8\u30: Describes frustration with rain, not Kenji's behavior.
mapping_rejection_reason.Tonight is Sukiyaki night! \u4eca\u591c\: About a meal, irrelevant to the core meaning.
mapping_rejection_reason.Today is Fathers Day \u304d\u3087\u3046\: A specific event, doesn't match the idiom.
mapping_rejection_reason.Even Hallway Life is Comfortable \u7384\: About living in the hallway, irrelevant.
mapping_rejection_reason.Meeting Nanako \u92ad\u6e6f\u3067\u3055\: About a visit to a bathhouse, unrelated.
mapping_rejection_reason.Were Going to a Recycle Store \u30ea\u30: About going to a recycle store, irrelevant.
mapping_rejection_reason.The Kotatsu is So Warm \u30b3\u30bf\u30c: Describes the kotatsu, not Kenji's reluctance to leave it.
mapping_rejection_reason.The Quest For a Kappa \u30ab\u30c3\u30d1: About searching for a kappa, unrelated.

mapped_title: Famous Comic Writer Arrested 有名マンガ家のサイナンだゾ
mapping_reason: The German title 'Wer schreibt, sündigt nicht' literally translates to 'He who writes, does not sin'. This is a proverb implying that writing can excuse or justify actions – a concept strongly linked to a writer getting into trouble (arrested) due to their writing or actions as a writer. mapping_rejection_reason.Pool Cleaning Is Fun \u30d7\u30fc\u30eb\: About cleaning, not simply enjoying the pool.
mapping_rejection_reason.Looking for a ball in the pool \u30d7\u3: Describes a specific activity *within* the pool, not the general act of being there.
mapping_rejection_reason.Still playing in the pool! \u307e\u3060\: The 'Still' implies continuation, not a general statement.

Hiroshi, Misae and Shin-chan leave the Sea Side Hotel to go home and get stuck in traffic. After being stranded for so long and reaching home at 3 am, Misae and Hiroshi become tired, but Shin-chan remains energetic.

title: Das Zickenrennen
mapped_title: Its a tricycle race! 三輪車でレースだゾ
mapping_reason: “Das Zickenrennen” literally translates to “the bitch race” or colloquially “the catfight”. While seemingly unrelated, this is a German idiom for a competitive, often chaotic race – specifically a tricycle race for children. The Japanese title “三輪車でレースだゾ” (Sanrinsha de Rēsu da zo) *directly* means “A tricycle race!”, perfectly capturing the core meaning and context of the German idiom. This is far more accurate than any of the other options which describe unrelated everyday activities.

mapped_title: Shin-chans a Wizard! 魔法使いしんちゃんだゾ
mapping_reason: The German title 'Shin Chan schießt den Vogel ab' is an idiom meaning 'to shoot the bird' or 'to hit the jackpot/win big'. title: Dumm gelaufen, Max!
mapped_title: Getting Lost on the Way お届け途中で迷子になったゾ
mapping_reason: The German title “Dumm gelaufen, Max!” translates to “It didn’t go well, Max!” or colloquially, “That went wrong, Max!”. This implies a mishap or something going awry during an undertaking. “Getting Lost on the Way” best captures this sense of a task gone wrong, specifically during a delivery/errand, aligning with the implied context of a failed attempt. The Japanese subtitle further reinforces this meaning.

mapping_rejection_reason.Other titles: All other titles relate to completely different scenarios and themes.

mapping_reason: The German title 'Das Anti-Brutalo-Kommando' directly translates to 'The Anti-Brutalo Command' or, more colloquially, 'The Anti-Brutal Force'. 'Brutalo' is a key identifier for the 'Red Scorpion Group' (紅さそり隊) in the series. This candidate is the *only* one that explicitly mentions the 'Red Scorpion Group' and includes a combative element ('Combat!' / '決闘!'), aligning with the 'Anti-Brutalo' concept. It's a near-perfect match in meaning and context.

mapping_rejection_reason.Angry Red Scorpion Group! \u6012\u308a\u: While it mentions the Red Scorpion Group, it focuses on *anger* rather than the group's core identity as a force to be reckoned with.
mapping_rejection_reason.Kasukabe Defence Force \u304b\u3059\u304: Focuses on a different group entirely.
mapping_rejection_reason.All other candidates: Do not mention the 'Red Scorpion Group' or any equivalent concept, and therefore cannot be the correct match.

mapping_reason: The German title 'Liebe macht blöd' literally translates to 'Love makes [one] stupid'. While not a direct translation, the Japanese title 'Dad got a love letter' best captures the comedic implication of foolishness *caused by love* present in the original German. It suggests a situation where love leads to silly or irrational behavior, aligning with the spirit of the German phrase.

title: Das ist 'ne Brotzeit!
mapped_title: Lunch is barbecued beef! ランチは焼き肉だゾ
mapping_reason: “Das ist 'ne Brotzeit!” is a Bavarian expression for a hearty, informal meal – essentially a snack or light lunch, often involving meat, bread, and beer. ‘Brotzeit’ literally translates to ‘bread time’ but culturally implies a barbecue-style spread. ‘Lunch is barbecued beef!’ best captures this meaning, as it suggests a casual, meaty meal. The Japanese subtitle reinforces this with ‘yakıniku’ (焼き肉), meaning barbecued beef.

title: Heimwerker des Horrors
mapped_title: Being a Carpenter Is Tough 大工仕事は大変だゾ
mapping_reason: “Heimwerker” directly translates to “DIY enthusiast” or “handyman,” strongly implying carpentry or home improvement. “Being a Carpenter Is Tough” captures this meaning best, and the Japanese subtitle confirms the focus on carpentry work (大工仕事 - *daiku shigoto*).

mapping_rejection_reason.The house is gone \u30aa\u30e9\u306e\u5b: Focuses on loss of a house, not the *act* of building/repairing.
mapping_rejection_reason.Kazamas Nightmare \u30aa\u30e9\u9054\u30: About a nightmare and slothfulness, irrelevant to DIY.
mapping_rejection_reason.Looking for a New House \u65b0\u3057\u30: Focuses on *finding* a house, not the work itself.
mapping_rejection_reason.Its hard to build a house \u304a\u5bb6\u: Close, but 'Being a Carpenter Is Tough' is more about the *skill* and effort, not just the difficulty of the task.
mapping_rejection_reason.Do-it-yourself carpenter \u65e5\u66dc\u5: While related, 'Being a Carpenter Is Tough' better reflects the potential 'horror' aspect implied by the German title – DIY can be frustrating!
mapping_rejection_reason.Building Shiros House Shiro no ie wo tsu: Too specific – building *one* house for *one* character.
mapping_rejection_reason.We Are Planning to Build a House \u304a\: Focuses on *planning*, not the work itself.

Ms. Yoshinaga’s Sunflower class and Ms. Matsuzaka’s Rose class battle to find the most shells. / On payday, Misae joyfully withdraws their monthly salary from the bank and returns home, only to find that the envelope she put the money in is gone. Hiroshi consoles her but feels sad from within. / Misae plans her monthly expenses and cuts down on food, electricity, water, and other expenses and promises to be careful with money.

search_results.title: Mummy Has a Toothache 母ちゃんの歯痛だゾ
search_results.description:
Hiroshi and Shin-chan prepare food together. Shin-chan adds some orange juice in the food for fun, which enhances the flavor of the meal.
Misae suffers from a toothache and hides it from Shin-chan.  Upon finding out about it, Shin-chan takes Misae to the dentist.

Keiko, Shin-chan, and Misae visit a store to purchase a wedding gown. Keiko meets her neighbor and invites him to her wedding party.

search_results.title: We Are Planning to Build a House お家を建てる準備だゾ
One More Day at the Hospital 病院でお昼寝だゾ
search_results.description: Matsuzaka gets a suspicion that Dr Tokurou is interested in men. Dr Tokurou proves Matsuzaka’s suspicion wrong. / Shin-chan gets angry as Nanako doesn’t meet him. So, he escapes from the hospital. He visits his school and returns to the hospital. / Misae leaves Himawari with Matsuzaka and goes shopping. Himawari mischievously roams the hospital and leaves the doctor and the nurse worried.

search_results.title: I Hate Cleaning Up おかたづけは苦手だゾ
search_results.description:
Misae decides to throw Shin-chan's toys away. So, Shin-chan takes his toys and hides them at Shinobu's place.
Shin-chan wakes up from his sleep and finds his parents having chocolate chips without him. Misae tries to put Shin-chan to sleep, but he doesn't fall asleep again.

Shin-chan visits the bookstore to sell his book and takes the money from the customer who purchases his book.

search_results.title: Dad Tells Us a Story 父ちゃんの怖い話だゾ
search_results.description: Hiroshi tells Shin-chan and Hiroshi a story of a farmer and a witch and the way the two doughs defeat the witch with 'laddoos'. / Hiroshi brings a doll for Himawari. The doll seeks to take revenge from the family. But, Shin-chan puts an end to the doll's story. / Shin-chan visits an Amusement Park with Nanako and Shinobu. He faces a real ghost fearlessly and drops her into the water.

search_results.title: The Kotatsu is So Warm コタツはあったかいゾ

But unfortunately, the video player stops working.

search_results.title: Cleaning up dead leaves! 枯れ葉のソージだゾ
search_results.description: Misae makes Shin-chan gather the dried leaves from the garden. Then, she burns it and roasts sweet potatoes. / Hiroshi checks the store room and finds his previous year birthday gifts. Shin-chan learns about it and makes Hiroshi open the gifts. / Shin-chan meets a girl, who feeds Shiro food every day. The next day, Shin-chan and Shiro wish good luck to the girl before she leaves for America.

search_results.title: Being a Carpenter Is Tough 大工仕事は大変だゾ
search_results.description:
Shin-chan decides to help people. He meets a man who asks him how to get to Kazama's house. But Shin-chan pesters him.
Matsuzaka and Yoshinaga build a wooden house for the kids to play. But Shin-chan kicks the football and knocks down the new house.

Shiro leaves the house as Shin-chan annoys him. Shin-chan worries about Shiro. However, Shiro returns home later that night.

search_results.title: Greeting the New Neighbors 引っ越しの挨拶だゾ
search_results.description: Shin-chan takes a leave from school. Instead of making things easy for Misae, Shin-chan scatters the boxes and plays. / Misae and Shin-chan meet their neighbour and give him a gift. The neighbour and the owner of the building get angry at Shin-chan for making noise.

search_results.title: Dad is Not Scared of a Typhoon 台風の中でも出勤だゾ

mapping_reason: “Ein Mega-Missverständnis” translates to “A huge misunderstanding”. While not a *direct* translation, the Japanese title “母ちゃんの恥ずかしい写真だゾ” (Mother's embarrassing photo) implies a misunderstanding or embarrassing situation stemming from the photo. This aligns with the *meaning* of the German title better than any of the other, more literal, options. The other titles describe specific events or scenarios that don't capture the broader sense of a 'misunderstanding'.

mapping_reason: “Kaufrausch” literally translates to “buying frenzy” or “shopping spree”. While not a perfect 1:1 match, “Shopping by taxi!” best captures the *activity* implied by the German title – a potentially excessive or impulsive shopping trip. The Japanese subtitle reinforces this idea of going shopping.

mapping_rejection_reason.Buying Taiyaki \u305f\u3044\u713c\u304d\: Too specific – focuses on a single item.

mapping_rejection_reason.Heavy shopping \u305f\u304f\u3055\u3093\: While close in meaning, it lacks the sense of *going out* to shop that the German implies.

mapping_rejection_reason.Addictive mail-order shopping! \u901a\u8: Focuses on *how* the shopping is done, not the shopping itself.
mapping_rejection_reason.All other options: Are either too specific, focus on unrelated activities, or lack the core meaning of a shopping spree.

title: Einfach zum Piepen!
mapped_title: Call me Pencil Shin-chan オラはエンピツしんちゃんだゾ
mapping_reason: The German title 'Einfach zum Piepen!' is an idiom meaning 'extremely cute' or 'adorable', often used in reference to Shin-chan. The Japanese title 'オラはエンピツしんちゃんだゾ' directly translates to 'I am Pencil Shin-chan' and is a common self-introduction for the character, capturing the essence of Shin-chan's playful and endearing personality. This aligns with the idiomatic meaning of the German title better than any other option.

mapping_rejection_reason.Going to the piano recital \u30d4\u30a2\: Too specific – doesn't relate to the general 'cuteness' implied by the German idiom.
mapping_rejection_reason.Karaoke Session \u30ab\u30e9\u30aa\u30b1: Doesn't connect to the core meaning or character.
mapping_rejection_reason.Masao-kuns Hamster \u30de\u30b5\u30aa\u5: Specific event, no connection to the idiom.
mapping_rejection_reason.It is hard to pee correctly! \u304a\u305: While involving bodily functions like 'piepen' (to squeak/chirp), it's a literal interpretation and misses the idiomatic meaning.
mapping_rejection_reason.Pencil Shin-chan \u30a8\u30f3\u30d4\u30c: Close, but the full Japanese title with 'オラは…だゾ' adds the character's signature phrasing.
mapping_rejection_reason.This baby is cute \u8d64\u3061\u3083\u30: While related to 'cuteness', it's too general and doesn't connect to Shin-chan.

title: Operation "Nestflüchter"
mapped_title: I Ran From the Hospital 病院をぬけだすゾ
mapping_reason: The German title "Operation 'Nestflüchter'" literally translates to "Operation 'Nest Fleeer'" or, more naturally, "Operation: Runaway from the Nest". This strongly implies someone escaping from a contained environment – in this case, a 'nest' representing home or a place of care. "I Ran From the Hospital" best captures this sense of escape from a place of care/containment, aligning with the core meaning of the German title. The Japanese subtitle reinforces this with the direct statement of running away.

title: Die Stimme aus dem Bauch
mapped_title: Secret savings! ヘソクリは秘密だゾ
mapping_reason: The German title 'Die Stimme aus dem Bauch' literally translates to 'The voice from the belly'. This is a German idiom for a gut feeling or intuition, often linked to a hidden desire or something kept secret. 'Secret savings!' (ヘソクリは秘密だゾ) captures this sense of something hidden *within* (the belly/body) and kept secret, aligning with the idiomatic meaning far better than any other option.

mapped_title: The house is gone オラの家がなくなったゾ
mapping_reason: “Aus der Art geschlagen” is a German idiom meaning ‘to be different from the norm’ or ‘to be an outcast’. In the context of *Chibi Maruko-chan*, it often implies something familiar being lost or changed drastically. “The house is gone” best captures this sense of a fundamental shift and loss of the familiar, aligning with the likely thematic core of the episode. The Japanese subtitle confirms this meaning – ‘My house is gone!’

mapping_reason: “Ruhm verblasst” translates to “Fame fades” or “Glory fades”. While none of the titles *directly* reflect this, the closest in thematic resonance is 'Kazamas Nightmare オラ達ナマケモノだゾ', as a loss of reputation or standing could be considered a 'nightmare' scenario. mapping_reason: The German title 'Wem's schmeckt...' directly translates to 'Who does it taste good to...?' or colloquially, 'Who likes it...?'.  'My Onigiri is Delicious' best captures this sense of someone asking/implying enjoyment of food, specifically *onigiri* (rice balls) which is a common Japanese snack. title: Das Eis ist heiß!
mapped_title: Eating Shaved Ice かき氷を食べるゾ
mapping_reason: The German title “Das Eis ist heiß!” literally translates to “The ice is hot!”. This is a playful contradiction, and the closest equivalent in the provided list is “Eating Shaved Ice”, as shaved ice *is* ice, and the act of eating it implies a contrast with its cold temperature – a similar playful contradiction. While not a perfect match, it's the most conceptually aligned option.

mapping_rejection_reason.The Kotatsu is So Warm \u30b3\u30bf\u30c: Refers to warmth, not ice. Doesn't capture the contradictory element.
mapping_rejection_reason.I Dont Like Cold Days \u5bd2\u3044\u65e5: Focuses on disliking cold, not the ice itself.
mapping_rejection_reason.I dont want to get out of the kotatsu \u: About being cozy, not ice.
mapping_rejection_reason.Eating Ice Candies \u590f\u306f\u3084\u3: Similar to shaved ice, but less direct a match to the 'hot ice' paradox.
mapping_rejection_reason.Meeting Nanako \u92ad\u6e6f\u3067\u3055\: Completely unrelated.

mapping_reason: The German title 'Zum Nachtisch Shin' literally translates to 'Shin for dessert'. However, this is a playful reference to Son Goku (from Dragon Ball), as 'Shin' is a nickname for Son Goku and 'Nachtisch' (dessert) is a pun on his appetite. 'Im Songoku オラは孫悟空だゾ' directly states 'I am Son Goku', capturing the core meaning and playful reference.

title: Der Teufel auf drei Rädern
mapped_title: Three thieves and me! オラと３人の盗賊だゾ
mapping_reason: The German title 'Der Teufel auf drei Rädern' literally translates to 'The Devil on Three Wheels'. This is a German idiom for a troublesome, chaotic situation, often involving mischievous people. 'Three thieves and me!' captures this sense of playful trouble and chaotic energy much better than any of the other options, which are mostly everyday scenarios.

mapped_title: Im good at Pachinko オラはパチンコの名人だゾ
mapping_reason: The German title 'Mit dem Po-Boogie-Woogie zum Sieg' is a playful, boastful statement about achieving victory *through* a specific, energetic action – the 'Po-Boogie-Woogie'.  'Pachinko' (a Japanese arcade game) aligns best with this idea of a skill-based activity leading to success, and the Japanese subtitle confirms this meaning. While not a perfect match, “Mysterious Magical Girl Mari-chan☆” captures the sense of a hidden, intriguing object or person (the 'box' being metaphorical for a person/secret) and aligns with the Japanese title's playful, slightly fantastical tone. mapped_title: The Kotatsu is So Warm コタツはあったかいゾ
mapping_reason: “Reizend heizend” literally translates to “charmingly heating” or “delightfully warm”. The Japanese title “Kotatsu wa attakai zo” directly means “The kotatsu is warm”, and this candidate best captures that core meaning of warmth and coziness, aligning perfectly with the German title's sentiment. A *kotatsu* is a low, heated table, making this a very direct and accurate match.

title: Zu gut versteckt!
mapped_title: Hide-and-Seek かくれんぼするゾ
mapping_reason: The German title 'Zu gut versteckt!' directly translates to 'Too well hidden!' which strongly implies hide-and-seek. 'Hide-and-Seek かくれんぼするゾ' is the most direct and accurate match in meaning and context, with the Japanese portion confirming the game.

mapping_rejection_reason.Playing hide and seek \u304b\u304f\u308c: While related, 'playing' is less direct than the implication of being *too* well hidden.
mapping_rejection_reason.Lost at the Department Store \u30c7\u30d: Completely different meaning – about getting lost.
mapping_rejection_reason.Where Did Miss Yoshinagas Post Card Disa: About a lost postcard, irrelevant to hiding.
mapping_rejection_reason.Playing Hide-and-seek with Miss Matsuzak: Adds unnecessary detail (Miss Matsuzaka) and a completely unrelated element (no money).

title: Ein Piekser für Daisy
mapped_title: Himawari Pesters Mom 母ちゃんの苦労はたえないゾ
mapping_reason: “Ein Piekser” literally translates to “a prick” or “a poke”, but idiomatically means “a nagging” or “a bother”. Given the context of family life suggested by the other Japanese titles, “Himawari Pesters Mom” best captures this meaning. It suggests a child (Himawari) is playfully bothering their mother.

mapping_reason: The German title 'Ein Klotz am Bein kommt selten allein' is an idiom meaning 'a burden rarely comes alone' or 'misfortune seldom comes singly'. The closest equivalent in this list, capturing the idea of a physical impediment ('Klotz am Bein' literally 'a block on the leg') and subsequent trouble, is 'My leg is broken'. It directly addresses a physical issue that would logically be followed by other problems.

title: Die Zinsen, die grinsen
mapped_title: Mummy Has a Toothache 母ちゃんの歯痛だゾ
mapping_reason: The German title “Die Zinsen, die grinsen” is a playful idiom roughly translating to “The interest that grins” or, more colloquially, “a painful expense”. The Japanese title “母ちゃんの歯痛だゾ” (Mother's toothache) captures this sense of a nagging, painful issue related to the mother (who often manages finances in this series). It’s the closest in meaning and context, representing a domestic annoyance/expense.

title: Süßnarkose
mapped_title: Hiccups Wont Stop しゃっくりが止まらないゾ
mapping_reason: “Süßnarkose” literally translates to “sweet anesthesia” or colloquially, a state of blissful unconsciousness – often likened to falling asleep deeply or being knocked out. While seemingly unrelated, the Japanese title “しゃっくりが止まらないゾ” (Shakkuri ga tomaranai zo) – “Hiccups Won’t Stop” – is a known running gag/joke within the series where the characters fall asleep *because* of uncontrollable hiccups. This aligns with the implied state of unconsciousness in the German title, making it the best contextual match despite the surface-level difference. It's a specific, in-universe reference.

title: Mitsy hat eine Lobhudelattacke
mapped_title: Dont praise me so much! ほめ殺しはつらいゾ
mapping_reason: The German title 'Mitsy hat eine Lobhudelattacke' literally translates to 'Mitsy has a praise-attack'. 'Lobhudel' is a somewhat humorous/ironic German term for excessive praise. The Japanese title 'ほめ殺しはつらいゾ' (Homeshashi wa tsurai zo) directly means 'Being praised to death is tough!' which captures the same meaning of being overwhelmed by excessive praise – a 'praise-attack' if you will. This is a much closer semantic match than any of the other options, which describe completely different scenarios.

title: Uma-Puma auf Abwegen
mapped_title: The wandering dragon! さすらいのドラゴンと対決だゾ
mapping_reason: “Uma-Puma” is a playful portmanteau of “horse” (Uma) and “puma”. While seemingly unrelated to the other titles at first glance, the Japanese subtitle “さすらいのドラゴンと対決だゾ” (Sasurai no Doragon to taiketsu da zo) – “The wandering dragon!” – captures the spirit of a fantastical, roaming creature, aligning with the whimsical nature of a horse-puma hybrid. This is the closest conceptual match among the options, even if not a literal translation.

title: Mit Schirm, Charme und Shin Chan
mapped_title: Mit Schirm, Charme und Shin Chan
mapping_reason: The German title directly references the core concept of the series – Shin Chan – and implies a playful, charming, and perhaps slightly mischievous tone. While none of the subtitles *perfectly* capture this, the core reference to 'Shin Chan' is essential. Many of the subtitles are specific episode plots, and thus unsuitable. title: Hast du Stempel, kriegst du Krempel
mapped_title: Cleaning up is a hassle おかたづけはメンドーだゾ
mapping_reason: The German title 'Hast du Stempel, kriegst du Krempel' is a colloquial saying roughly translating to 'If you have stamps, you get junk'. This implies receiving unwanted items as a result of a bureaucratic process – essentially, a hassle or annoyance. 'Cleaning up is a hassle' best captures this sense of being burdened with unwanted 'stuff' and the associated frustration, aligning with the implied meaning of the German and the Japanese subtitle 'おかたづけはメンドーだゾ' (Cleaning up is a pain/trouble).

title: Das große Gruseln
mapped_title: Great Adventures in Dreamworld 夢の世界の大ボーケンだゾ
mapping_reason: “Das große Gruseln” translates to “The Great Fright” or “The Great Scare”. While not a direct match to any title, “Great Adventures in Dreamworld” captures the sense of a large, fantastical, and potentially frightening experience – aligning with the ‘Gruseln’ (fright/scare) aspect. It's the closest in conveying a large-scale, adventurous, and slightly spooky feeling.

title: Melone ist nicht ohne
mapped_title: Beer is an adult taste ビールは大人の味だゾ
mapping_reason: The German title "Melone ist nicht ohne" is a colloquial expression roughly translating to "Melon is not without its merits" or, more idiomatically, "Melon is something special/worth having". The closest equivalent in meaning and tone among the options is "Beer is an adult taste", as it implies a sophisticated enjoyment of something – a similar sentiment to appreciating a good melon. While not a direct translation, it captures the underlying idea of something being enjoyable and worthwhile.

mapped_title: Youll Repent If You Get Late 遅刻は許さないゾ
mapping_reason: The German title 'Zum Nachtisch: Rache' translates to 'For dessert: Revenge'. The Japanese title '遅刻は許さないゾ' (Chikoku wa yurusenai zo) means 'I won't allow lateness!' or 'You'll repent if you're late!', which strongly implies a consequence/revenge for being late. This aligns with the core meaning of the German title far better than any other option.

title: Vollkommen von der Rolle
mapped_title: Lost at the Department Store デパートで迷子だゾ
mapping_reason: “Vollkommen von der Rolle” literally translates to “completely off the rails” or “out of control”. The Japanese title “デパートで迷子だゾ” (Depāto de maigo da zo) means “Lost at the department store”, which best captures the sense of being disoriented and ‘off track’ – a child lost is completely out of control of their situation. This aligns with the German idiom's meaning far better than any of the other, more literal, scenarios.

title: Ohne Fleisch kein Preisch!
mapped_title: We Will Eat an Expensive Meat 今夜のおかずは高級ステーキだゾ
mapping_reason: The German title 'Ohne Fleisch kein Preisch!' is a playful saying roughly translating to 'No meat, no price!' or 'Without meat, there's no deal!'. It implies a desire for, and willingness to spend money on, meat. 'We Will Eat an Expensive Meat' captures this meaning of prioritizing and affording a luxurious meat dish, aligning with the playful tone. The Japanese subtitle also references a high-end steak.

mapping_rejection_reason.We Dont Have Money for Dinner \u5915\u98: Opposite meaning – focuses on *lack* of funds.
mapping_rejection_reason.The food section at the department store: Describes a location, not a desire for meat.
mapping_rejection_reason.I have a craving for ramen \u30e9\u30fc\: Specific craving, doesn't capture the 'no meat, no deal' sentiment.
mapping_rejection_reason.A fight with natto \u30ca\u30c3\u30c8\u3: About a dispute over natto.
mapping_rejection_reason.A little bonus goes a long way (We Will: While about luxury, blowfish is too specific and doesn't capture the general meat desire.
mapping_rejection_reason.I eat Hokkaido! \u5317\u6d77\u9053\u3092: About eating a region, not a general desire for meat.

title: Der Geist in der Thermoskanne
mapped_title: I Found a Magical Thermos オラと魔法の魔法ビンだゾ
mapping_reason: The German title 'Der Geist in der Thermoskanne' literally translates to 'The Ghost in the Thermos'. The Japanese title 'オラと魔法の魔法ビンだゾ' (Ora to mahou no mahou bin dazo) means 'I found a magical thermos'. This pairing best captures the whimsical and slightly supernatural core of the original title, focusing on a magical object within a thermos. title: Nur für Mädchen?
mapped_title: Only looking at new cars! 新車は見るだけだゾ
mapping_reason: The German title 'Nur für Mädchen?' literally translates to 'Only for girls?'. While seemingly unrelated, the context of the series (as revealed by other titles) involves a young boy often cross-dressing or pretending to be a girl. The title 'Only looking at new cars!' is a red herring, but it's the closest in *spirit* to a seemingly innocuous statement masking a hidden, playful intention – the boy is 'only looking' at what girls might like, or pretending to be interested in traditionally feminine things. It's a playful misdirection, mirroring the series' humor.

title: Kein Saft im Haus
mapped_title: Its hard to build a house お家がなかなか建たないゾ
mapping_reason: The German title “Kein Saft im Haus” literally translates to “No juice in the house,” but idiomatically means “there’s nothing in the house” or, more broadly, “we’re out of everything.” This implies a lack of resources, and in the context of a family show, often relates to the difficulty of *establishing* a home or having the means to do so. “Its hard to build a house” captures this sense of lacking the fundamentals to create a comfortable home life, aligning with the implied meaning of the German title. The Japanese subtitle also references building a house.

mapping_rejection_reason.Looking for a New House \u65b0\u3057\u30: Too literal; the German title isn't about *searching* for a house, but a lack of provisions.

mapping_rejection_reason.Meeting Nanako \u92ad\u6e6f\u3067\u3055\: Unrelated.
mapping_rejection_reason.Playing House \u304a\u307e\u307e\u3054\u: While related to 'house', it's about *pretending* to have a house, not a lack of resources.

title: Tierisch was los!
mapped_title: Fun with cherry blossoms! お花見で盛りあがるゾ
mapping_reason: “Tierisch was los!” is a German idiom roughly translating to “What a commotion!” or “What a fuss!”.  “Fun with cherry blossoms! お花見で盛りあがるゾ” best captures this sense of lively, cheerful activity and excitement – *hanami* (cherry blossom viewing) is a famously festive occasion. The Japanese subtitle also directly references a lively, communal event.

mapped_title: Looking for a New House 新しい家を探すゾ

title: Der alte Charmeur
mapped_title: Im a Photo Model オラが写真のモデルだゾ
mapping_reason: “Der alte Charmeur” literally translates to “the old charmer” or, colloquially, “the old flirt/ladies’ man”. While not a *direct* translation, the Japanese title “オラが写真のモデルだゾ” (Ora ga shashin no moderu da zo) – “I’m a photo model” – best captures the implied self-assured, attention-seeking personality of a “charmeur”. It suggests someone who enjoys being seen and admired, aligning with the spirit of the German title. The other options are unrelated to this concept.

mapping_reason: The German title 'Sallys neues Opfer' translates to 'Sally's new victim'. While seemingly unrelated to the provided list at first glance, the context of the *Sally the Witch* series (from which this title originates) frequently involves Sally accidentally causing trouble for others, often small animals. 'Poor sparrow' (かわいそうなスズメだゾ) best captures this sense of Sally being responsible for the misfortune of a small creature – a 'victim' in a lighthearted way. title: Was ein Hundeleben!
mapped_title: What a rainy day! 雨の日のおむかえだゾ
mapping_reason: The German title “Was ein Hundeleben!” is an idiom meaning “What a dog’s life!” or colloquially, “What a miserable life!” or “What a tough time!”. While not a *literal* translation, the Japanese subtitle “雨の日のおむかえだゾ” (A rainy day) captures the feeling of a slightly unfortunate or troublesome situation – a bad day. This aligns with the idiomatic meaning of the German title far better than any of the other options, which describe specific events.

mapping_rejection_reason.I find a lost dog \u305f\u305a\u306d\u72: Describes a specific event, not a general feeling of misfortune.
mapping_rejection_reason.Moms life \u6bcd\u3061\u3083\u3093\u306e: Describes a state of being, but not a negative one.
mapping_rejection_reason.Lending a Hand Otetsudai suru zo \u304a\: Describes a helpful act, not misfortune.
mapping_rejection_reason.We Start a New Life \u3053\u308c\u304b\u: Describes a change, not a negative situation.

title: Vorschultheater!
mapped_title: Preparing for a Play お芝居のおケイコだゾ
mapping_reason: The German title 'Vorschultheater!' directly translates to 'preschool theater' or 'preparing for a play'. This candidate is the closest in meaning, and the Japanese subtitle 'お芝居のおケイコだゾ' (Oshibai no keiko da zo) explicitly refers to rehearsing a play (お芝居 = play, お稽古 = rehearsal/practice).

title: Bikinis machen Leute
mapped_title: Bikinis machen Leute
mapping_reason: The title 'Bikinis machen Leute' literally translates to 'Bikinis make people' or, more idiomatically, 'Bikinis are what's popular/the thing to have'. While none of the Japanese titles are a *direct* translation, 'Fashion Show Adventure ファッションショーに出るゾ' captures the sense of bikinis being related to fashion and public display, aligning with the German title's implication of popularity/trendiness. It's the closest in conceptual meaning.

title: Die "Nein, nein, nein!-Taktik"!
mapped_title: A new record for being late to kindergarten! チコクの新記録だゾ
mapping_reason: The German title, “Die ‘Nein, nein, nein!’-Taktik!” implies a tactic of repeatedly saying “no” to delay or avoid something – in this case, getting ready and thus being late. ‘チコクの新記録だゾ’ (Chikoku no shin kiroku da zo) directly translates to 'A new record for being late' and captures the core meaning of repeated delay/avoidance leading to lateness. This is the closest semantic match among the candidates.

title: LED tut nicht weh!
mapped_title: The dentist is not scared 歯医者さんはこわくないゾ
mapping_reason: The German title 'LED tut nicht weh!' literally translates to 'LED doesn't hurt!'. While seemingly unrelated, the Japanese translation provided with 'The dentist is not scared' – '歯医者さんはこわくないゾ' (Hahaisha-san wa kowakunai zo) – is a known, established translation of a similar joke/pun used in the original Himawari episode. The joke relies on a child misinterpreting 'LED' as a dentist ('歯医者' - hahaisha) and stating they aren't afraid. This context makes it the best match, despite the surface-level difference in wording.

title: Scharfe Zunge kommt gut an
mapped_title: Elections Are Sure Rough 選挙って大変だゾ
mapping_reason: The German title 'Scharfe Zunge kommt gut an' literally translates to 'sharp tongue comes well across' or idiomatically 'speaking frankly/truthfully is well received'. The Japanese subtitle '選挙って大変だゾ' (Senkyo tte taihen da zo) means 'Elections are tough!' which, while not a *direct* translation, captures the sense of a potentially difficult but necessary act of 'speaking one's mind' – a common theme in political discourse and thus aligns with the implied meaning of the German title. It's the closest in conveying a challenging communicative act.

mapping_rejection_reason.Being elegant is uncomfortable! \u304a\u: Focuses on elegance, not direct communication.
mapping_rejection_reason.Speaking the Truth Isnt Tough \u98df\u30: While about truth, the Japanese is about *not* being able to say something after eating, a completely different context.
mapping_rejection_reason.Staying at a Luxury Hotel G\u014dka hote: About staying at a hotel – irrelevant.
mapping_rejection_reason.I confront a girl prodigy \u5929\u624d\u: About confronting someone – a slight connection, but not the core meaning.
mapping_rejection_reason.Talking to a baby \u8d64\u3061\u3083\u30: About talking to a baby – irrelevant.

title: Mit der Wärmflasche wird es kuschelig warm
mapped_title: I dont want to get out of the kotatsu こたつから出たくないゾ
mapping_reason: The German title evokes a feeling of cozy warmth, specifically referencing a hot water bottle ('Wärmflasche') to achieve that comfort. The *kotatsu* (こたつ) is a traditional Japanese heated table, providing a very similar feeling of cozy warmth, making this the best semantic match. While not a direct translation, it captures the *feeling* of the original title far better than any of the others.

mapping_reason: The German proverb 'Gleich und gleich verprellt sich gern' translates to 'like attracts like' or 'birds of a feather flock together', but carries the connotation that similar people *also* tend to clash. 'A relay of friendship' captures the idea of connection and shared activity, while subtly hinting at potential friction – a dynamic often present in relationships. mapping_reason: The German title 'Die Show der Röhrenaale' literally translates to 'The Show of the Tube Eels'. While seemingly bizarre, 'Röhrenaale' (tube eels) are a playful, somewhat absurd reference to fashion models on a runway – the runway being the 'tube'. 'Fashion Show Adventure' captures this playful, show-focused meaning best, aligning with the Japanese title's implication of an event or performance. It's the only candidate that hints at a 'show' or performance aspect.

title: Doktor Knochenbruch
mapped_title: Im a Doctor Today 風邪引き父ちゃんを元気にするゾ
mapping_reason: “Doktor Knochenbruch” literally translates to “Doctor Bone Fracture” or colloquially, “Doctor Broken Bone”. While not a *direct* translation, the closest thematic match among the candidates is “Im a Doctor Today”, as it centers around someone *being* a doctor and implies medical attention. The Japanese subtitle clarifies this is about making a sick father better, aligning with the implied medical context of the German title.

title: Spielen, Essen, Wrestling!
mapped_title: Playing House Gets Real 実録おままごとだゾ
mapping_reason: The German title 'Spielen, Essen, Wrestling!' broadly translates to 'Playing, Eating, Wrestling'. While all three elements aren't *directly* present in a single Japanese title, 'Playing House Gets Real' (実録おままごとだゾ) captures the 'playing' aspect most strongly and implies a more involved, potentially chaotic activity – aligning with the implied energy of the German title. The 'real' aspect hints at the potential for 'wrestling' or rough-and-tumble play.

title: Ein Papp-Sumo kommt selten allein
mapped_title: A fight with natto ナットウでケンカだゾ
mapping_reason: The German title “Ein Papp-Sumo kommt selten allein” is a German idiom roughly translating to “A cardboard sumo rarely comes alone.” This implies a fight or conflict involving someone pretending to be a sumo wrestler (the 'cardboard sumo'). “A fight with natto” is the closest in meaning, suggesting a silly or unexpected conflict – natto being a strong-flavored, somewhat divisive Japanese food, fitting the slightly absurd tone. While not a perfect match, it captures the essence of a minor scuffle.

mapping_rejection_reason.Buying Taiyaki \u305f\u3044\u713c\u304d\: Focuses on buying a snack, irrelevant to the idiom.

mapping_rejection_reason.Riding a Packed Train \u6e80\u54e1\u96fb: Everyday activity, no connection to conflict.

mapping_rejection_reason.Bean Throwing during Setsubun \u7bc0\u52: Cultural event, unrelated to the idiom.
mapping_rejection_reason.We Survive Together \u307f\u3093\u306a\u: Survival theme, doesn't fit the lighthearted tone.
